name: Oleyl adapalenate
lead: Oleyl adapalenate (marketed as Adapinoid) is described in the literature as a third-generation retinoid and a pro-drug of adapalene, formed by joining adapalene to an oleyl group [1]. It is used in cosmetic skincare creams aimed at photoaging, positioned as a retinoid with better tolerability.

Published evidence is limited to a small number of studies. A 2024 randomized, double-blind, 12-week trial of 48 people compared 0.5% oleyl adapalenate cream with 0.5% retinol cream and reported greater wrinkle improvement with oleyl adapalenate and better tolerability [1].

paras: One published trial, a prospective, double-blind, randomized head-to-head study (NCT05778760), compared 0.5% oleyl adapalenate with 0.5% retinol in 48 participants over 12 weeks, with visits at weeks 4, 8 and 12. Wrinkle severity, the primary outcome, improved by 9.45% with oleyl adapalenate and 4.11% with retinol, a between-group difference reported as significant. Pigment intensity fell by 3.88% and 3.15% respectively, without a significant difference between groups. Oleyl adapalenate reduced facial erythema by 13.39%, whereas retinol produced no significant change, and oleyl adapalenate was reported to be better tolerated at all follow-up visits [1]. The study was small and short, and the authors themselves note that research on the compound is scarce [1].
The authors describe oleyl adapalenate as a pro-drug of adapalene, a synthetic retinoid, and suggest this design may maintain efficacy while improving tolerability relative to retinol [1].

timeline.event: Head-to-head randomized trial versus retinol published [1].

card.summary: A newer adapalene-ester cosmetic retinoid with one small 2024 trial suggesting better wrinkle results and tolerability than retinol.

quick.overview:
Oleyl adapalenate is a cosmetic ingredient described as a pro-drug of the acne and photoaging retinoid adapalene.

A single 12-week trial of 48 people found it improved wrinkles more than retinol and was better tolerated.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a pro-drug that releases adapalene, a retinoid, in the skin.
quick.risks: Little safety research exists beyond the one trial, which reported better tolerability than retinol.
